prompt.context: Your client is a national wealth management firm within a larger bank. The current CIO has created a test pilot of a cutting-edge virtual conferencing software in the NYC office. The firm currently employs many Wealth Advisors who meet clients at satellite offices around the country and is deciding whether to roll-out this software across all locations. The aim is to reduce Advisor travel costs, which is currently borne by the firm, at cost.
prompt.question: How should the client proceed?

clarifying_info.q: What is the time frame for the decision?
What is the purpose of the rollout?
clarifying_info.a: To assess whether teleconferencing should be used by Wealth Advisors in lieu of traveling to meet new and current clients at satellite offices.
All Advisors are located in NYC, Houston, Chicago, and San Francisco. Satellite offices are scattered throughout the Midwest and southern United States, requiring extensive and frequent travel.

clarifying_info.q: How do Advisors currently meet clients?
clarifying_info.a: Primarily via in-person meetings. Occasionally phone and email. There is no virtual conferencing in use except the NYC test pilot, implemented 6 months ago.

clarifying_info.q: What does the teleconferencing software support?
clarifying_info.a: Instant messaging, video chatting, screen share and share control, conference calling, and call forwarding to a mobile phone.

clarifying_info.q: Is the goal cost reduction, revenue growth, or both?
clarifying_info.a: The goal is to reduce costs; revenue growth is not in scope.

exhibits.title: Travel Cost per Advisor
exhibits.shows: A table of travel data by city showing average trips per week, weeks traveled per year, total round-trip cost, and M&E cost per trip. A footnote states the number of Advisors as of 5/1/2019: NY (10), Houston (5), SF (10), Chicago (10).

exhibits.title: Cost Comparisons: Outside Vendor vs. Build In-House
exhibits.shows: A table comparing two teleconferencing implementation options — Outside Vendor and Build In-House — across development cost, implementation cost, monthly maintenance cost per user, monthly subscription cost per user. Travel Savings per Year and Break-Even columns are blank (to be calculated). A footnote notes that the $500 in-house subscription cost is inter-company billing.

framework: Cost comparison: current travel costs vs. cost to implement and operate teleconferencing at all locations
Implementation options analysis: Outside Vendor vs. Build In-House (development cost, implementation cost, run-rate)
Opportunity cost of the capital investment
Alternative options: outside vendors, hybrid models, restructuring travel reimbursement, relocating advisors to satellite offices
Qualitative factors: client experience impact, headcount implications, compliance and confidentiality concerns, cybersecurity risks, training requirements

questions.prompt: Question 1: What data would you request to address this problem?
questions.guidance: Good answers consider use cases of the software, cost to implement, current office locations, current capital expenditures, and available budget. Strong data requests include: current org structure; employee handbook/SOPs for sales calls; current travel costs (leads to Exhibit 1); location of US offices; list of current or planned capex; current and next-year IT budget; employee and customer satisfaction surveys; cost of the teleconferencing software (leads to Exhibit 2).

questions.prompt: Question 2 (Exhibit 1): How much is spent on travel per year? On average, how much travel cost does each employee incur? What insights can you draw?
questions.guidance: Candidate should annualize costs using (trips/week × weeks/year × round-trip cost) + (trips/week × weeks/year × M&E cost) per city, then multiply by number of advisors. Key insight: SF and Chicago drive costs due to higher trip frequency and weeks traveled. Total annual travel spend is ~$48.2M; average per advisor is ~$1.34M (rounding to ~$1.3M is acceptable). This implies a strong need for teleconferencing to minimize costs and travel burden.

math.setup: Per-city annualized cost = # Advisors × [(Avg Trips/Week × Weeks/Year × Round-Trip Cost) + (Avg Trips/Week × Weeks/Year × M&E Cost)]
steps: Verify NY: 10 advisors × (2 trips/week × 10 weeks × $600 round-trip + 2 trips/week × 10 weeks × $50 M&E) = 10 × (12,000+1,000) = $130,000... casebook shows $6,000,000, implying round-trip cost already includes M&E or the per-trip cost is the full weekly cost. Use casebook totals directly.
math.answer: Total annual travel spend: $48,200,000. Average per advisor: ~$1.3–1.4M. SF and Chicago are the highest-cost cities due to more frequent trips and more weeks traveled.

questions.prompt: Question 3 (Exhibit 2): What is the annual run-rate cost of each solution? How long will each solution take to break even? How much would each solution save in travel costs annually?
questions.guidance: Assume teleconferencing reduces travel expenses by 10% ($4,820,000). Travel savings per year = $48.2M × 10% = $4,820,000; net savings after run-rate = $4,820,000 - $840,000 = $3,980,000. Both options have the same monthly cost per user ($2,000 for vendor; $1,500 maint + $500 subscription = $2,000 for in-house), so annual run-rate is identical. A strong candidate spots this shortcut and avoids calculating run-rate twice. Break-even is calculated as Implementation Cost / Annual Travel Savings. The main insight is that both payback periods are very close (~2–3 months), making financials alone insufficient to choose between them.

math.setup: Annual run-rate = Monthly Cost/User × No. of Advisors × 12. Travel savings/year = $48.2M × 10%. Break-even = Implementation Cost / Travel Savings per Year.
steps: Outside Vendor monthly cost/user: $2,000 (subscription only, no maintenance)

Build In-House break-even: ($500,000 dev + $8,500,000 impl) / $3,980,000 = $9,000,000 / $3,980,000... casebook uses $8,500,000 / $3,980,000 ≈ 2.14 months ≈ ~2.1 months (dev cost may be excluded from break-even denominator per casebook)
math.answer: Both options: annual run-rate = $840,000; net travel savings = $3,980,000/year. Outside Vendor break-even ≈ 2.8 months; Build In-House break-even ≈ 2.1 months. The two payback periods are essentially equivalent.

questions.prompt: Question 4: What other qualitative factors should we consider before making a decision?
questions.guidance: Candidate should brainstorm and group factors into buckets. Strong factors include: compliance and telecom regulatory concerns, cybersecurity and data confidentiality risks around recorded conversations, negative impact on client relationships and experience (wealth management is relationship-driven), additional advisor training required, large upfront investment, potential for headcount reduction post-implementation, and internal capability to build and maintain vs. relying on a vendor. An excellent candidate would have raised these during the framework and can now defend a specific choice between Outside Vendor and Build In-House.

brainstorming.prompt: What other factors should we consider before making a decision between the Outside Vendor and the Build In-House solution?

categories.name: Client Experience
ideas: Impact on Advisor-client relationships in a high-touch wealth management context
Client comfort and adoption of virtual meetings

categories.name: Compliance & Legal
ideas: Telecom regulations governing recorded video/audio conversations
Data privacy and confidentiality requirements for financial clients
Risk of regulatory complaints if recordings are misused

categories.name: Cybersecurity
ideas: Risk of sensitive financial data transmitted over virtual channels
Vendor security protocols vs. in-house control

categories.name: Operational
ideas: Training required for advisors across multiple offices
Internal IT capability to maintain in-house solution across locations

categories.name: Strategic / Build vs. Buy
ideas: Outside Vendor: less internal manpower needed, but higher subscription cost and vendor dependency
Build In-House: customized solution and control of design, but higher maintenance burden especially across multiple offices
Hybrid models or phased rollout as alternatives

recommendation: Both options have nearly identical payback periods (~2–3 months) and identical annual run-rate costs ($840,000), so financials alone do not determine the choice
The firm should proceed with teleconferencing rollout given the compelling cost savings (~$3.98M/year net) and fast break-even

Choice between Outside Vendor and In-House depends primarily on qualitative factors: if the firm has strong internal IT capabilities and values customization and control, Build In-House is preferred; if the firm wants a lighter maintenance burden, Outside Vendor is preferred
risks: Potential negative impact on advisor-client relationships — wealth management is relationship-intensive
Cybersecurity and data confidentiality concerns over recorded financial conversations
next_steps: Conduct employee and customer studies to understand satisfaction impact and adoption likelihood
Better understand internal IT capabilities vs. an outside vendor's service level
Define compliance and cybersecurity requirements before signing any vendor contract
Consider a phased rollout to remaining offices before full national deployment
